panels.title: Throughput
panels.description: Commands served per second, across all clients.

panels.title: p99 latency
panels.description: The number that matters. A mean hides the request that waited behind an fsync or a compaction; one request in a hundred being slow is noticed by every user who makes a hundred requests.

panels.title: Connections
panels.description: Client connections currently open.

panels.title: Keyspace hit rate
panels.description: Fraction of lookups that found a key. A collapse here means the cache has stopped doing its job, whatever the latency graph says.

panels.title: Disk footprint
panels.description: Total bytes the engine occupies, data files plus write-ahead log.

panels.title: Uptime
panels.description: Seconds since the server started.

panels.title: Command throughput
panels.description: Commands and errors per second.

panels.title: Command latency percentiles
panels.description: Computed from the exported histogram's cumulative buckets. The gap between p50 and p99.9 is the interesting quantity: a wide gap means something intermittent is stalling requests, usually background maintenance.

panels.title: SSTables per level
panels.description: The clearest single signal of compaction health. Level 0's tables overlap, so every lookup must check all of them -- a level 0 that keeps growing means the compactor is losing to the write rate, and reads degrade before anything else does.

panels.title: Engine operations
panels.description: The fsync line is worth watching against the write line: the ratio between them is the durability policy made visible. One fsync per write is the strict policy; far fewer means group commit is amortising them.

panels.title: Disk footprint over time
panels.description: Split out because they mean different things. The log is the durability record for data not yet in a table and shrinks when a memtable flushes; the data files are the database itself.

panels.title: Compaction write rate
panels.description: Write amplification made visible: bytes rewritten by compaction, against the bytes clients actually sent. This is what levelled compaction trades away in exchange for cheap reads and low space amplification.

panels.title: Block cache hit rate
panels.description: Blocks are cached after decompression, so a hit saves both the read and the decompression. A low rate means the working set is larger than the cache.

panels.title: Bloom filter effectiveness
panels.description: Every 'ruled out' is a disk read that never happened. The ratio between the two lines is the measured false-positive rate: at the default 10 bits per key it should sit near 1%, and a rate far above that points at the filter rather than the workload.

panels.title: Memory
panels.description: Working set includes the memtable, the block cache, the Bloom filters and every SSTable index held open; the managed heap is the part the GC can move.

panels.title: Garbage collections
panels.description: Gen-2 collections are the ones that hurt: they are the likeliest managed explanation for a p99.9 spike that the storage metrics cannot account for.

panels.title: Thread pool and network
panels.description: A growing work-item queue means the server is accepting faster than it can serve, which shows up as latency before it shows up as errors.

panels.title: Role
panels.description: 1 for the leader, 0 for a follower. Exactly one series should sit at 1: two at once would mean two leaders, which is the failure the whole protocol exists to prevent.

panels.title: Term
panels.description: Increments on every election. A term climbing steadily with no node failures means something is repeatedly disrupting elections -- a flapping network, or a node that thinks it is a voter and is not.

panels.title: Voters
panels.description: Voting members of the current configuration. Learners are counted separately.

panels.title: Learners
panels.description: Non-voting members: replicated to, counted in no quorum. Normally a transient state on the way to a promotion.

panels.title: Quorum size
panels.description: Acknowledgements needed to commit. This, not the voter count, is what the cluster's failure tolerance is derived from -- and it is what rises the moment a learner is promoted.

panels.title: Membership change
panels.description: 1 while a change is in its joint phase, needing a majority of both the old and new configurations. Lingering at 1 is a problem: the cluster then tolerates fewer failures than either configuration alone.

panels.title: Snapshot size
panels.description: Size of the state-machine image the log is truncated behind.

panels.title: Log entries
panels.description: Entries the log holds after snapshotting -- what a restart actually has to replay, as opposed to the total it has ever written.

panels.title: Replication progress
panels.description: Committed, applied and log end per node. A node whose applied index trails the others is the one at risk of falling far enough behind to need a whole snapshot rather than ordinary catch-up.

panels.title: Log range and snapshots
panels.description: A first index above 1 means the prefix has been folded into a snapshot. The gap between first and last index is the log that still exists; everything before it is covered by the snapshot.

panels.title: Elections and membership
panels.description: Elections started but not won are the interesting line: a node campaigning repeatedly and losing is disrupting a healthy cluster without being able to replace it.

panels.title: Snapshot activity
panels.description: An installed snapshot means a follower was too far behind to catch up from the log, so it was sent the whole dataset. Frequent installs suggest the snapshot threshold is too eager for the replication lag.

panels.title: Pre-vote outcomes
panels.description: A lost pre-vote is an election that did not happen: the term was never incremented and no other node had to react, so this line going up is the mechanism working. What it reports is that some node repeatedly believes it should lead and the cluster disagrees -- a flapping link, or a node that does not know it was removed. Compare it against elections started on the left: with pre-vote on, that one should stay flat while this one absorbs the churn.

panels.title: Replication lag by role
panels.description: Entries each peer trails the leader's commit index by. The roles mean different things: a voter lagging slows every commit, because commitment waits on a quorum of acknowledgements, while a learner lagging only delays its promotion. A learner's lag should fall steadily after it is admitted -- a flat line means catch-up has stalled and promoting it would hand a vote to a node that cannot answer.

title: KestrelCache
description: Server throughput and tail latency on top, storage-engine internals in the middle, and replication at the bottom. The engine panels explain the latency panels; the Raft panels explain which node is answering at all.
